Region: Nile Valley, northeast Africa
History: Unified under the pharaohs around 3100 BC, Egypt endured through the Old, Middle, and New Kingdoms, building an empire that stretched into Canaan and Nubia. It later fell to Assyria, Persia, Greece, and Rome, but its monuments and records outlasted every conqueror.
Culture: Egyptians wrote in hieroglyphs, built pyramids and temples on a monumental scale, and advanced medicine, astronomy, and administration. The annual Nile flood made farming predictable and supported one of the ancient world's most stable states.
Religion: Egypt worshipped many gods, chief among them Ra, Osiris, Isis, and Horus, and treated the pharaoh as a divine king. Belief in judgment after death shaped its tombs, mummification, and funerary texts.
BibleConnection: Abraham visited Egypt in famine; Joseph rose to vizier there; Israel spent centuries in Egypt before the Exodus, the defining deliverance of the Old Testament. Later kings allied with Egypt, refugees fled there after Jerusalem's fall, and Joseph and Mary took the infant Jesus to Egypt to escape Herod.
RelatedPeople: Abraham; Joseph, Son of Jacob; Moses; Aaron; Miriam; Zipporah; Mizraim
RelatedEvents: Abram in Egypt; Joseph and His Brothers; The Exodus and the Red Sea

Region: Northern Levantine coast: Tyre, Sidon, Byblos
History: Phoenician city-states dominated Mediterranean trade, founding colonies as far as Carthage. They were never a single empire, but their ships, timber, and purple dye made them indispensable partners of Israel's kings.
Culture: Phoenicians are credited with spreading the alphabet that became the ancestor of Greek and Latin scripts. Their cedar timber built temples and palaces across the region.
Religion: Phoenician religion honored Baal, Astarte, and Eshmun, with rites Scripture condemns. Jezebel, daughter of Sidon's king, brought Baal worship to Israel's court with devastating effect.
BibleConnection: Hiram of Tyre supplied cedar and craftsmen for Solomon's temple; Jezebel's marriage to Ahab imported Baal worship; Jesus visited the region of Tyre and Sidon, where a Syrophoenician woman's faith drew his praise.

Region: Syria, centered on Damascus
History: Aramean kingdoms, chiefly Damascus, rose after the Bronze Age collapse and contested the land east and north of Israel. Aram fought Israel under Ben-Hadad and Hazael, allied with it at times, and finally fell to Assyria in 732 BC.
Culture: Aramaic, the language of the Arameans, became the lingua franca of the Near East and the everyday language of Jesus' world. Aramean trade and diplomacy connected Mesopotamia with the Levant.
Religion: Arameans worshipped Hadad (Rimmon), the storm god, among others. Naaman, commander of Aram's army, was healed of leprosy after washing in the Jordan at Elisha's word.
BibleConnection: Aram is both enemy and neighbor in Kings: wars with Ahab and Jehoram, the siege of Samaria, and Naaman's healing, which showed God's mercy reaching beyond Israel.

Region: Highlands east of the Dead Sea
History: Moab, descended from Lot according to Genesis, was a small kingdom east of the Dead Sea that alternated between war and uneasy peace with Israel. King Mesha's revolt against Israel is recorded both in 2 Kings 3 and on his own victory stele.
Culture: Moabites farmed the highlands and controlled the King's Highway trade route. Their language was closely related to Hebrew, and their royal inscriptions are among the closest parallels to biblical Hebrew.
Religion: Moab worshipped Chemosh, to whom kings offered sacrifices, including, at least once, a king's own son in wartime desperation. Ruth the Moabitess, who left Moab to follow Naomi's God, became an ancestor of David.
BibleConnection: Balak of Moab hired Balaam to curse Israel; Ruth came from Moab; and the plains of Moab are where Moses died within sight of the Promised Land.
RelatedPeople: Ruth; Naomi; Boaz; Lot; Balaam; Balak
RelatedFinds: Mesha Stele (Moabite Stone); Balaam Inscription (Deir Alla Inscription)

Region: East of the Jordan, around modern Amman
History: The Ammonites, descended from Lot's son Ben-Ammi, held the land east of the Jordan around their capital Rabbah. They clashed with Israel from the judges through David, who captured Rabbah, and survived as a small state into the Persian period.
Culture: Ammon shared the language and material culture of its neighbors Moab and Israel, and its capital Rabbah was a fortified trade center on the King's Highway.
Religion: Ammon worshipped Molech (Milcom), whose rites included child sacrifice, which the Law of Moses strictly forbade. Solomon's Ammonite wives brought Molech's worship into Jerusalem itself.
BibleConnection: Jephthah defeated Ammon; Saul's first victory as king was against Ammon's siege of Jabesh-gilead; David's war with Ammon frames the Bathsheba story.

Region: South of the Dead Sea, from the Arabah to the Red Sea
History: Edom, descended from Esau, occupied the rugged land south of the Dead Sea and controlled the copper mines of the Arabah and the Red Sea port of Ezion-geber. Edom refused Israel passage in the wilderness, warred with Judah's kings, and was later displaced by the Nabataeans; its people, the Idumeans, included Herod the Great's family.
Culture: Edomites built their capital at Bozrah and the mountain stronghold of Petra's region, living by mining, herding, and tolls on the trade routes between Arabia and the Mediterranean.
Religion: Edom worshipped Qos as its chief god. The prophet Obadiah pronounced judgment on Edom for standing by, and even joining in, when Jerusalem fell.
BibleConnection: Edom is Esau's land, the brother-nation that became Israel's rival: the birthright story, the refused passage, and Obadiah's oracle all turn on that brotherhood.

Region: Anatolia (modern Turkey), with influence into Syria and Canaan
History: The Hittites built one of the Bronze Age's great empires from their capital Hattusa, fighting Egypt to a standstill at Kadesh and concluding the earliest surviving peace treaty. After the empire's fall around 1200 BC, smaller Neo-Hittite states survived in Syria for centuries.
Culture: Hittites pioneered iron-working, codified laws, and drew up detailed treaties and covenants. Their treaty forms — preamble, history, stipulations, blessings and curses — closely parallel the structure of the biblical covenants.
Religion: Hittite religion embraced a thousand gods, led by the storm god Tarhunt and the sun goddess Arinna. Their rituals and legal texts show a world of oaths, purity rules, and treaty obligations.
BibleConnection: Hittites appear in the patriarchal stories: Ephron the Hittite sold Abraham the cave of Machpelah, and Uriah the Hittite was the husband of Bathsheba. Hittite treaty patterns help explain the shape of God's covenants with Israel.

Region: Northern Mesopotamia, capital Nineveh
History: Assyria rose from a city-state on the Tigris to the Near East's first true empire, conquering the northern kingdom of Israel in 722 BC and deporting its people. Its siege of Jerusalem in 701 BC failed, and Nineveh itself fell to Babylon and Media in 612 BC.
Culture: Assyrians built vast palaces and libraries — Ashurbanipal's library at Nineveh preserved the Epic of Gilgamesh — and administered their empire with roads, officials, and mass deportations.
Religion: Assyria's chief god was Assur, with Ishtar of Nineveh and other gods of war and fertility. Its kings presented conquest as divine mandate, and their annals record cruelty as policy.
BibleConnection: Assyria is the rod of God's judgment in Isaiah and the repentant city of Jonah's preaching. Its fall, celebrated by Nahum, showed that even the mightiest empire answers to God.
RelatedEvents: Jonah and Nineveh; Hezekiah and Sennacherib's Invasion; Fall of Samaria
RelatedFinds: Sennacherib Prism (Taylor Prism); Lachish Reliefs; Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III; Kurkh Monolith of Shalmaneser III

Region: Southern Mesopotamia, capital Babylon
History: Babylon, heir of Sumer and Akkad, reached its height under Hammurabi and again under Nebuchadnezzar, who destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC and carried Judah into exile. Cyrus of Persia took the city in 539 BC without a battle.
Culture: Babylon gave the world Hammurabi's law code, advanced astronomy and mathematics, the Hanging Gardens tradition, and the ziggurat — the stepped temple tower behind the Babel story.
Religion: Babylon worshipped Marduk above a large pantheon, with Ishtar, Shamash, and Nabu among the chief gods. Its priests read omens in the stars and livers, a practice Daniel's God repeatedly overruled.
BibleConnection: Babylon is both a place and a symbol in Scripture: the tower of Babel, the exile that reshaped Israel's faith, Daniel's court, and the 'Babylon' of Revelation standing for every proud power opposed to God.
RelatedEvents: The Tower of Babel; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Daniel in the Lions' Den
RelatedFinds: Babylonian Chronicle (Nebuchadnezzar's Chronicle); Code of Hammurabi; Nabonidus Cylinder; Jehoiachin's Rations Tablets; Al-Yahudu Tablets

Region: Iran plateau to the Mediterranean, capital Susa and Persepolis
History: Cyrus the Great founded the Persian Empire, the largest the ancient world had yet seen, stretching from India to Greece. His edict let the Jewish exiles return and rebuild the temple; later kings Darius, Xerxes, and Artaxerxes framed the world of Ezra, Nehemiah, and Esther.
Culture: Persia administered its empire through satrapies, royal roads, and a policy of tolerance toward local customs and gods. Its postal system and coinage knit together peoples from three continents.
Religion: Persian kings promoted Ahura Mazda, the wise lord of Zoroastrian teaching, while tolerating the religions of their subjects. The empire's tolerance is what made the return from exile possible.
BibleConnection: Persia is the setting of the return: Cyrus's decree, the temple's rebuilding, Esther in Susa, and Nehemiah's wall. Isaiah calls Cyrus God's anointed, the pagan king who serves God's purpose.
RelatedPeople: Cyrus the Great; Mordecai; Nehemiah; Ezra; Elam
RelatedEvents: Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile; Esther Saves Her People; Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall; Rebuilding of the Temple; Ezra Reads the Law

Region: Greek mainland, Aegean islands, and Alexander's eastern empire
History: Greek city-states gave the West philosophy, drama, and democracy, and Alexander's conquests spread Greek language and culture across the East. After Alexander, his successors ruled the world of the Maccabees, and Greek became the language in which the New Testament was written.
Culture: Greece prized reason, rhetoric, athletics, and art, and its language became the common tongue of the eastern Mediterranean. The Septuagint, the Greek Old Testament, carried Scripture to the wider world.
Religion: Greeks worshipped Zeus, Athena, Apollo, and a host of gods on Olympus and in every city. Paul found Athens full of idols and an altar 'to an unknown god,' which became his opening to preach Christ.
BibleConnection: Daniel foresaw Greece as the goat that shatters Persia's ram; the New Testament was written in Greek; and Paul's missionary journeys carried the gospel through the Greek cities of Corinth, Athens, Philippi, and Ephesus.
RelatedEvents: Paul's Missionary Journeys; The Conversion of Paul
RelatedFinds: Gallio Inscription; Corinth Bema (Judgment Seat); Politarch Inscription; Erastus Inscription

Region: Italian peninsula to an empire around the Mediterranean
History: Rome grew from a city-state to a republic and then an empire that ruled the whole Mediterranean world, including Judea from 63 BC. Its roads, laws, and peace — the Pax Romana — form the backdrop of the entire New Testament.
Culture: Rome built roads, aqueducts, and cities on a scale never seen before, spread Latin law and citizenship, and absorbed Greek art and learning. Its engineering and administration held a vast empire together for centuries.
Religion: Romans worshipped Jupiter, Mars, and the emperor himself, whose cult demanded loyalty from every subject. Christians' refusal to call Caesar lord was one reason for their persecution.
BibleConnection: Jesus was born under Caesar Augustus's census, crucified under Pontius Pilate, and Paul appealed to Caesar and was imprisoned in Rome itself. The empire that killed the apostles also carried their message to the ends of the earth.
RelatedEvents: The Birth of Jesus; The Crucifixion; Paul in Rome
RelatedFinds: Pilate Stone; Herodium (Herod's Tomb); Ephesus Theater; Sergius Paulus Inscription

Region: Upper Nile, south of Egypt (modern Sudan)
History: Cush, son of Ham (Genesis 10:6) and father of Nimrod, is the biblical name for the Nubian kingdom the Greeks called Ethiopia. Kushite kings ruled Egypt as its Twenty-fifth Dynasty, and Cush appears throughout the prophets as a distant southern nation. The Ethiopian eunuch baptized by Philip (Acts 8) shows Cushites still traveling to Jerusalem to worship in the New Testament period. In English Bibles the people of Cush are also called the Ethiopians.
Culture: Kushites built pyramids at Meroe, worked iron, and traded gold, ivory, ebony, and exotic goods up the Nile to Egypt and beyond.
Religion: Kushites worshipped Amun and other gods of the Nile valley, with great temples at Napata and Meroe blending Egyptian and Nubian religion.
BibleConnection: From Nimrod's kingdom to the psalmist's promise that Ethiopia shall stretch out her hands to God (Psalms 68:31), Cush stands for the far south brought within God's reach — a theme completed when Philip baptizes the Ethiopian court official.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 10:6; Psalms 68:31; Isaiah 18:1; Isaiah 43:3; Ezekiel 29:10; Acts 8:27

Region: Southwestern Iran, east of Mesopotamia, around Susa
History: One of the ancient world's oldest kingdoms, Elam lay east of Babylon with its chief city at Susa. Chedorlaomer, king of Elam, led the coalition Abraham defeated to rescue Lot (Genesis 14). Elam later warred with Assyria, was absorbed into the Persian Empire, and Susa became a Persian royal capital. Elamites were among the peoples present at Pentecost.
Culture: Elamites spoke their own language, unrelated to Semitic or Indo-European tongues, built ziggurats and palaces at Susa, and traded across Mesopotamia and the Iranian plateau.
Religion: Elamites worshipped their own gods, chief among them Inshushinak, god of Susa, alongside a wider Mesopotamian pantheon.
BibleConnection: Beyond Chedorlaomer, Elam appears in judgment oracles (Isaiah 21:2; Jeremiah 49:34-39, which also promises a later restoration), in Ezekiel's lament over fallen nations, and in Daniel's vision, which takes place at Shushan in the province of Elam (Daniel 8:2).
KeyScriptures: Genesis 14:1; Isaiah 21:2; Jeremiah 49:34; Ezekiel 32:24; Daniel 8:2; Acts 2:9

TimePeriod: Conquest era through David's reign, c. 1400-1000 BC
Region: Geshur, east of the Sea of Galilee, bordering Bashan and Aram
History: Geshur was a small Aramean kingdom on Israel's northeastern border. Deuteronomy 3:14 notes that Geshur and Maacath were not driven out, and Joshua 12:5 and 13:13 record them as peoples left among Israel. Geshur became royal kin to David: Maacah, daughter of Talmai king of Geshur, was the mother of Absalom (2 Samuel 3:3), and after killing Amnon, Absalom fled to Geshur and stayed three years (2 Samuel 13:37-38). Geshur and Aram later took Havoth-jair from Israel (1 Chronicles 2:23). A separate southern group of the same name appears among David's raid targets in 1 Samuel 27:8; whether it is the same people is unclear.
Culture: A small border kingdom, strong enough to shelter a royal fugitive and to intermarry with David's house, but never a great power. Its kings are named individually (Talmai) rather than as a dynasty.
Religion: No distinct Geshurite religion is described; as an Aramean kingdom it shared the religious world of Aram.
BibleConnection: Geshur gave David a wife and Absalom a refuge, tying Israel's royal house to the Aramean borderlands and shaping the rebellion that followed.
KeyScriptures: Deuteronomy 3:14; Joshua 12:5; Joshua 13:13; 2 Samuel 3:3; 2 Samuel 13:37-38; 1 Chronicles 2:23

Region: Canaan and the land of Israel, eastern Mediterranean coast
History: Israel begins with Jacob, renamed Israel after wrestling with God (Genesis 32). His twelve sons became the twelve tribes. After slavery in Egypt, the Exodus under Moses and the conquest under Joshua gave them the land of Canaan. Under David and Solomon Israel was one kingdom; after Solomon it split into Israel in the north and Judah in the south. Assyria destroyed the northern kingdom in 722 BC and Babylon destroyed Judah in 586 BC, but a remnant returned under Cyrus and rebuilt Jerusalem and the temple. In the New Testament the name Israel still denotes God's covenant people, and Paul wrestles with Israel's place in God's purposes in Romans 9–11.
Culture: Israelite culture was built around the family, the tribe, and the covenant law given at Sinai. Agriculture, shepherding, and later town life shaped daily existence; festivals at the tabernacle and then the temple marked the year, and the law governed worship, justice, and neighbourly life.
Religion: Israel worshipped the LORD alone, in contrast to the many gods of its neighbours. The covenant at Sinai, the sacrificial system, the priesthood, and the prophets' call to justice and exclusive loyalty to God define its religion. Idolatry and the worship of Baal and other gods are presented throughout the history as the recurring breach of that covenant.
BibleConnection: Israel is the central people of the whole Bible: the Old Testament is largely their story, and the New Testament presents Jesus as Israel's Messiah, born of Judah, and the church as grafted into Israel's covenant promises.
KeyScriptures: Genesis 32:28; Genesis 35:10; Exodus 19:5-6; Deuteronomy 7:6-8; 1 Kings 12:16-20; 2 Kings 17:6; Ezra 1:1-4; Romans 9:4-5
RelatedPeople: Abraham; Isaac; Jacob; Joseph, Son of Jacob; Moses; Aaron; Miriam; Joshua; Samuel; Ezra; Nehemiah; Jesus
RelatedPlaces: Canaan; Egypt; Goshen; Jericho; Jerusalem; Samaria; Babylon; Mount Sinai; Jordan River
RelatedEvents: The Exodus and the Red Sea; The Ten Commandments; Crossing the Jordan; The Walls of Jericho; The Kingdom Divides; Fall of Samaria; Fall of Jerusalem and the Exile; Cyrus's Decree and Return from Exile; Ezra Reads the Law; Nehemiah Rebuilds the Wall; Rebuilding of the Temple
RelatedFinds: Merneptah Stele; Tel Dan Stele (House of David); Black Obelisk of Shalmaneser III; Kurkh Monolith of Shalmaneser III; Cyrus Cylinder; Jehoiachin's Rations Tablets

Region: Western Asia Minor (modern Turkey), around Sardis
History: Lud, son of Shem (Genesis 10:22), is the ancestor of the Lydians, whose kingdom in western Asia Minor grew rich on trade and is traditionally credited with the first coined money. Under kings such as Alyattes and Croesus the kingdom flourished until Cyrus of Persia conquered it in 546 BC. In the prophets, Lud's bowmen serve Tyre and fall with Egypt's allies.
Culture: Lydians were traders and craftsmen, famed for textiles, dyes, and gold from the Pactolus river, and for an early coinage that spread across the ancient world.
Religion: Lydians worshipped Anatolian deities, including the mother goddess Cybele, alongside Greek and Near Eastern gods of the region.
BibleConnection: Lydia appears as Lud among the nations in Ezekiel's lament over Tyre (Ezekiel 27:10), among the peoples falling with Egypt (Ezekiel 30:5), and among the nations to which escapees are sent (Isaiah 66:19). The Lydia of Acts 16 is a different matter: she is an individual woman from Thyatira, not the nation, and is not cited here.

TimePeriod: Conquest era through the divided monarchy
Region: Maacah, northeast of Bashan, bordering Geshur
History: Maacah was a small kingdom northeast of Bashan. Like Geshur, it was not driven out in the conquest (Deuteronomy 3:14; Joshua 13:13), and Joshua 12:5 marks it on the border of Og's kingdom. In David's wars the king of Maacah sent a thousand men to fight with the Ammonites against Israel (2 Samuel 10:6, 8). Eliphelet, son of Ahasbai the Maachathite, served among David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23:34), and Jaazaniah the Maachathite was among the captains who came to Gedaliah after Jerusalem's fall (Jeremiah 40:8).
Culture: A small border kingdom, able to field troops for a coalition war yet small enough that its men served individually in David's and Gedaliah's companies.
Religion: No distinct Maacathite religion is described.
BibleConnection: Maacah appears at both ends of the monarchy: fighting David with Ammon, then standing with Gedaliah's remnant after the exile began.
KeyScriptures: Deuteronomy 3:14; Joshua 12:5; Joshua 13:13; 2 Samuel 10:6; 2 Samuel 23:34; Jeremiah 40:8

Region: Northwestern Iran, south of the Caspian Sea
History: The Medes were an Iranian people whose kingdom, under kings such as Cyaxares, joined Babylon in destroying Nineveh in 612 BC. Cyrus of Persia conquered Media around 550 BC, and the two peoples formed the Medo-Persian Empire, whose law was famously unchangeable (Daniel 6:8). Darius the Mede took Babylon after its fall and ruled it while Daniel served at court.
Culture: Medes were famed as horsemen and warriors, and their court dress and customs deeply influenced the Persian Empire that absorbed them.
Religion: The Medes practiced an early form of Iranian religion; later tradition connects their priestly class, the magi, with Zoroastrian teaching, though the text itself does not describe their worship.
BibleConnection: The Medes are God's named instrument against Babylon (Isaiah 13:17; Jeremiah 51:11, 28), and Daniel's career spans their rule: the lions' den is dated to Darius the Mede, and Daniel's vision of the ram names the two horns as the kings of Media and Persia (Daniel 8:20).
KeyScriptures: Isaiah 13:17; Jeremiah 51:11; Daniel 5:28; Daniel 6:8; Daniel 8:20; Daniel 9:1; Acts 2:9
RelatedEvents: Daniel in the Lions' Den; Pentecost

Region: Southwestern Arabia (modern Yemen)
History: Sheba, the Sabaean kingdom of southwestern Arabia, grew wealthy on the frankincense and myrrh trade. Its queen visited Solomon to test his wisdom and left laden with gifts (1 Kings 10). Sabeans raided Job's livestock (Job 1:15), Sheba's merchants traded with Tyre (Ezekiel 27:22), and the prophets picture Sheba's gold and incense coming to Jerusalem (Psalms 72:10; Isaiah 60:6).
Culture: Sabaeans built an irrigation civilization around the Marib dam, carved inscriptions in their own South Arabian script, and ran caravans carrying incense, spices, gold, and precious stones across Arabia.
Religion: Sabaeans worshipped astral deities, chief among them the moon god Almaqah and a sun goddess, with temples and offerings tied to their irrigation state.
BibleConnection: Sheba's queen is the Bible's great example of a foreign ruler seeking Israel's wisdom, and Jesus pointed to her — the queen of the south — as a witness against his own generation (Matthew 12:42).
KeyScriptures: Genesis 10:28; 1 Kings 10:1; Job 1:15; Psalms 72:10; Isaiah 60:6; Ezekiel 27:22; Matthew 12:42

Region: Mesopotamia, centered on Akkad
History: Sargon of Akkad, a court official who seized power, conquered the Sumerian city-states and built the first empire in history, stretching from Elam to the Mediterranean. His dynasty held Mesopotamia for about 150 years before the empire fell to Gutian pressure and internal revolt.
Culture: Akkadians spoke a Semitic language that became Mesopotamia's lingua franca. Their scribes adapted Sumerian cuneiform, and their art — victory stelae and cylinder seals — set the imperial style later empires copied.
Religion: Akkadians worshipped the Mesopotamian pantheon, chief among them Anu, Enlil, and Ishtar. Naram-Sin went further, declaring himself a living god, a claim later kings echoed and Scripture answers.
BibleConnection: Genesis 10:10 names Accad (Akkad) among the first cities of Nimrod's kingdom in Shinar, placing the Akkadian heartland on the Bible's map of the earliest post-Flood powers. The Babel story is set in the same land of Shinar where Akkad rose.

Region: Armenian highlands around Lake Van
History: A mountain kingdom of fortresses and irrigation canals that rivaled Assyria for two centuries. Its kings inscribed their deeds on rock faces around Lake Van. Sennacherib's sons fled to the land of Ararat — Urartu — after murdering their father, and the kingdom fell to Median and Scythian pressure around 590 BC.
Culture: Urartians were master metalworkers and fortress builders, damming mountain streams into canals that watered their highland fields.
Religion: Urartu's chief god was Haldi, god of war, honored at the rock sanctuary of Musasir, which Sargon II of Assyria famously sacked.
BibleConnection: Urartu is the land of Ararat of 2 Kings 19:37 and Isaiah 37:38, refuge of Sennacherib's murderers, and the mountains of Ararat where the ark rested (Genesis 8:4) are Urartu's highlands.

Region: Syria and Mesopotamia to Persia, capital Antioch
History: Seleucus I, one of Alexander's generals, took the eastern part of Alexander's empire and founded a dynasty ruling from Antioch. His successors fought the Ptolemies for a century over the Levant. Antiochus IV Epiphanes tried to stamp out Jewish worship, sparking the Maccabean revolt, and Rome ended the empire when Pompey annexed Syria in 63 BC.
Culture: Seleucids spread Greek cities, language, and coinage across the East. Antioch became one of the ancient world's great cities and later the launching point of Paul's missionary journeys.
Religion: Seleucid kings promoted Greek gods and ruler cult. Antiochus IV set up a pagan altar in the Jerusalem temple and banned circumcision and Sabbath observance — the crisis behind the Maccabean revolt and the feast of Hanukkah.
BibleConnection: Daniel 11's kings of the North are the Seleucids, whose wars with the Ptolemaic kings of the South fill the chapter's long prophecy. Antiochus IV is the chapter's vile person (Daniel 11:21) and a foreshadowing of later persecutors. Antioch, the Seleucid capital, is where believers were first called Christians (Acts 11:26).

Region: Egypt, capital Alexandria, with Cyprus, Cyrene, and at times the Levant
History: Ptolemy I, another of Alexander's generals, seized Egypt and founded a Greek dynasty that ruled from Alexandria for nearly three centuries. The Ptolemies fought the Seleucids for the Levant in the Syrian Wars, and Alexandria's library and lighthouse became wonders of the world. The last ruler, Cleopatra VII, allied with Rome's losers and died as Octavian took Egypt in 30 BC.
Culture: Ptolemaic Alexandria was the ancient world's center of learning — its library, its scholars, and its Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures, the Septuagint, which carried the Old Testament to the Greek-speaking world and shaped the New Testament's quotations.
Religion: Ptolemies blended Greek and Egyptian worship, presenting themselves as pharaohs and gods, while Alexandria's large Jewish community worshipped at its synagogues and produced the Septuagint.
BibleConnection: Daniel 11's kings of the South are the Ptolemies, matched against the Seleucid kings of the North, and the Septuagint made in their capital is the Bible most New Testament writers quote.

Region: Northern Arabia and the Negev, capital Petra, with Damascus at times
History: Arab traders who built Petra, carving tombs and temples into rose-red cliffs and growing rich on the incense route between Arabia and the Mediterranean. Their kings, named Aretas or Obodas in turn, held Damascus in the first century AD, and Rome annexed the kingdom as Arabia Petraea in AD 106.
Culture: Nabataeans engineered desert water — cisterns, channels, and dams — that let Petra flourish in arid land, and their carved facades still stand as one of the ancient world's marvels.
Religion: Nabataeans worshipped Arabian deities, chief among them Dushara, god of the mountains, alongside Allat and al-Uzza.
BibleConnection: Aretas, king of the Nabataeans, held Damascus when Paul escaped the city in a basket through a window in the wall (2 Corinthians 11:32-33) — the kingdom is the backdrop of Paul's first escape.

Region: Iran plateau to Mesopotamia
History: Parthian horsemen from the steppe east of the Caspian took Persia from the Seleucids and built an empire Rome never conquered — Crassus died at Carrhae in 53 BC, and Augustus settled for a frontier on the Euphrates. Parthia ruled Mesopotamia through the whole New Testament period until the Sassanians replaced it in AD 224.
Culture: Parthians were famed mounted archers — the Parthian shot, firing backwards at full gallop — and their kings ruled through vassal lords rather than a centralized bureaucracy.
Religion: Parthians tolerated many faiths across their empire. Zoroastrian tradition was strong in Iran, while Mesopotamian and Greek cults continued in the west.
BibleConnection: Parthians were among the peoples at Pentecost (Acts 2:9), hearing the gospel in their own tongue. Some readers see Parthia behind Revelation's kings from the east (Revelation 16:12), though the text does not name them.
